That's probably the best answer I have seen on here.

Whenever you go to a website you're essentially asking a computer somewhere on the internet (called a server) to send you the data about that website. But servers are only machines and they can only handle so much traffic. A DDoS attack (standing for Distributed Denial of Service) exploits this by sending millions of requests to the server and overwhelming it, making it nearly impossible for legitimate users to request access to webpages.

Disclaimer: I'm not sure I have a solid understanding of it myself but I'll explain what I think it is...

Imagine you set up a lemonade stand or something. But your rival (or just some jerk) doesn't want to see you do well, so they come along and place like 96 orders of lemonade. You can't handle that since you're used to giving out one or two lemonades. So you freak out and spill your lemonade and then everything gets sticky.

And that is how you get ants.

It's more like they waste your time by asking, "How much is the lemonade? Where do you get your ingredients? What made you want to start a lemonade stand?" without ever ordering an actual lemonade. And then they get their friends to do it too. And the people in line behind them who actually want lemonade can't get them promptly, so they leave.

You own a bar. You want to serve real customers to serve drinks and make money.

Someone who doesn't like you goes around the neighborhood and gets a bunch of homeless people to go into your bar and order water. Hundreds of them. Far more than the normal number of customers in your bar. They suck up all your time and energy, and while you can serve a real customer here and there, most of the people who place orders are placing orders for water, and you can't keep up.

That's basically a DDoS. Someone uses naughty computer code to hijack other computers and control them to all visit a website at the same time. The website can't serve data to the real people who want it because it's busy serving data to hijacked computers.

So that 5 second delay that checks if we're a real person? That's like the bouncer the bar hires to keep homeless people from coming in.

I like all the answers so far but I'll bring another perspective.

All exchanges have a cost. It could be resources such as electricity or it could be available time. Regardless, every time we communicate we exchange things of value.

There are ways of making that exchange very unbalanced. One side can offer very little and take way too much. They can take so much that no one else can have a chance to exchange anything. This is the denial.

They way it works is some one takes advantage of a flaw or more commonly misuses the way that an exchange, the internet for example, works so that it costs them very little and costs the other person very much.

In the specific instance of using bots for a DDoS, the attacker spends a little money to rent 10's or 100's of thousands of computers that have been previously infected with software that allows a remote user to issue commands and sends as much traffic to a site as possible for the purpose of denying anyone else the ability to connect to that site.

So you have a server. This server takes incoming requests from users and processes them.

On an average day let's say you have 500 users an hour coming in and requesting that the server do something. The server is built (its hardware and software) to handle a bit more than 500 to account for abnormal days, so let's say it can handle 1000 requests an hour if need be.

Then one day some guy with 100 networked computers decides to have a laugh. So he sets up an automated program to have each computer request something from the server every second. Suddenly the server is trying to handle 6000 requests a minute. The server can't handle that... so it lags, slows down and even crashes.
